title: Fairness in Machine Learning: Lessons from Political Philosophy
abstract: What does it mean for a machine learning model to be `fair', in terms which can be operationalised? Should fairness consist of ensuring everyone has an equal probability of obtaining some benefit, or should we aim instead to minimise the harms to the least advantaged? Can the relevant ideal be determined by reference to some alternative state of affairs in which a particular social pattern of discrimination does not exist? Various definitions proposed in recent literature make different assumptions about what terms like discrimination and fairness mean and how they can be defined in mathematical terms. Questions of discrimination, egalitarianism and justice are of significant interest to moral and political philosophers, who have expended significant efforts in formalising and defending these central concepts. It is therefore unsurprising that attempts to formalise `fairness' in machine learning contain echoes of these old philosophical debates. This paper draws on existing work in moral and political philosophy in order to elucidate emerging debates about fair machine learning.

claims.text: Certain mathematical measures of fairness in machine learning are impossible to satisfy simultaneously except in rare and contrived circumstances.
Mental state accounts of discrimination do not naturally transfer to algorithmic decision-making contexts because algorithms lack conscious intentions, animosity, or disrespect.
Statistical discrimination uses statistical generalizations about group characteristics to infer individual attributes or future behaviors.
The term fairness as used in machine learning is best understood as a placeholder for a variety of distinct normative egalitarian considerations.
Representational fairness focuses on equal representation of identity categories in digital cultural artifacts rather than the direct distribution of decision outcomes to individuals.

limitations.text: Demographic parity is a blunt fairness metric that fails to account for explainable differences grounded in legitimate factors.
Existing fair machine learning approaches focus on a narrow, static set of legally prescribed protected classes without context.

Translating complex egalitarian theories into practical ML tasks is difficult because required contextual data regarding personal responsibility, life history, and socio-economic context is rarely captured in available datasets.

future_work.text: Develop contextually sensitive fairness approaches in machine learning that integrate historical and sociological factors beyond legally protected categories.

methodologies.name: Conceptual mapping of political philosophy to fair machine learning
methodologies.description: Theoretical review mapping concepts from moral and political philosophy—including mental state accounts, luck egalitarianism, spheres of justice, and deontic justice—onto formal machine learning fairness metrics.
